judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: B is slightly better because it uses the workload dependency manifest directly and accurately frames the required sdkmanager package IDs and their linkage to the installed workload. A is also strong and more actionable in its MSBuild snippet, but muddles required versus optional/additional dependencies (notably NDK) and relies on a referenced rather than supplied standalone script. B's extra Microsoft-OpenJDK-only assertion is unsupported by the shown manifest, but does not outweigh its core advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately frames this as a Microsoft-JDK vendor requirement, supplies the correct JAVA_HOME remediation, and avoids endorsing Temurin. A includes the Microsoft installation option but its diagnosis and alternate Temurin-based fix are materially misleading.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B better satisfies the requested workload-version reconciliation and Android package consistency plan with concrete discovery and installation commands. It does include some overbroad claims about non-Microsoft JDKs and assumes a latest SDK/workload set, but these do not outweigh its stronger rubric coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: B more fully meets the requested macOS MAUI setup requirements: it provides concrete officially sourced components, dynamic compatibility discovery, a reproducible pinned workload install, and the critical Xcode update warning. A is broadly useful but misses several rubric-critical constraints and actively suggests workload update.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the underlying issue: MAUI can auto-detect the JDK, the warning is not itself proof of a problem, and explicitly selecting Temurin is inappropriate when Microsoft OpenJDK is required. A has useful cautions about hardcoded paths and GUI shell environments, but its erroneous endorsement of Temurin and unnecessary configuration guidance materially weaken the result.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, methodical, and avoid the major pitfalls. B is better on the JDK criterion (correctly specifying Microsoft OpenJDK, where A recommends generic distro OpenJDK) and provides more authoritative manifest-based version discovery plus explicit warnings about meta-workload and repair. A's InstallAndroidDependencies approach is elegant and pragmatic, but B's coverage of the specific rubric points is more complete. The gap is meaningful mainly on the JDK item but modest overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are thorough, well-structured, and dynamically discover versions. B leveraged the dotnet-maui-doctor skill to align with authoritative guidance: it discovers workload versions via the dotnet CLI, correctly emphasizes Microsoft OpenJDK (the only supported distribution) with recommended-version discovery from WorkloadDependencies.json, and installs the exact Android packages MAUI requires. A is excellent and cleaner on the 'maui' workload point and uses the InstallAndroidDependencies MSBuild target elegantly, but it does not discover workload-set versions and lets the JDK come implicitly from VS. B's approach is more rigorous on the JDK/Android dependency discovery, which are the trickier correctness aspects. Overall B is slightly better, mainly due to its stronger workload-version discovery and JDK handling, despite the minor 'maui android' vs 'maui' quibble.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, well-structured, and cover the full setup with verification and version-discovery guidance. The decisive difference is accuracy of version discovery: B actually pulled the authoritative WorkloadDependencies.json from NuGet packages, yielding precise, verified requirements (MAUI 10.0.20, Android 36.1.69, JDK 17.0.14 with range, Xcode >=26.6). A relied on docs/release pages and appears to conflate the SDK feature band (10.0.401) with the MAUI workload version, and states some figures (Xcode 26.6, MAUI 10.0.101) that are less clearly sourced. B also more explicitly emphasizes Microsoft OpenJDK exclusivity and warns against update/repair. A is somewhat more approachable (VS Code emulator workflow, Android Studio option) and covers the editor/extension setup a bit more fully, but B's superior correctness on the version-discovery criterion—the crux of the task—makes it the better answer overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration

A gives generally competent advice but takes the opposite stance on the core issue—it recommends keeping/setting JAVA_HOME (just resolved dynamically) and never explains auto-detection, missing the central point that the SO fix is unnecessary. Although A did more research, correctness against the rubric matters more, and B is more accurate to actual .NET MAUI behavior.

A also adds useful QueryProperty parameter-receiving code, but on the core structural correctness B is right and A is wrong, making B slightly better overall.

B is superior on the key explanatory criterion by naming the D_FAULT_ prefix and the reorder/add instability trigger, and adds a realistic two-tab example plus the await note. A is correct but less specific.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add light/dark mode support using AppThemeBinding
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides correct C# using the actual SetAppThemeColor/SetAppTheme<T> extension methods, plus a cleaner resource-based/implicit-style approach and useful notes on UserAppTheme. A's C# is technically wrong (assigning an AppThemeBinding object to a Color property does not work), which is the key point the rubric asks about.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid common theming mistakes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct and cover all rubric criteria. B is slightly better because it provides a more complete, robust implementation: a proper App-level theme swap that removes/re-adds only the active theme dictionary, correctly warns against using MergedDictionaries.Clear() (which A recommends and would wipe MAUI's other resources), and wires up RequestedThemeChanged. A's Clear() approach is a genuine pitfall. A does add extra useful mentions of AppThemeBinding and UserAppTheme, but B's core swapping guidance is safer and more correct.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create custom themes with ResourceDictionary switching
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect and respond to system theme changes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fully satisfy all four rubric criteria with correct, working code. B goes further with valuable extras: an EffectiveTheme helper distinguishing system vs effective theme, proper ILogger-based logging (the task explicitly required logging the change), full ResourceDictionary/AppThemeBinding examples, and the critical Android ConfigChanges.UiMode note that prevents activity restart on theme change — a real-world gotcha. A is more concise and correct (and notes MainThread marshaling and unsubscription, which B omits), but B addresses the logging requirement more directly and covers the platform-specific detail that matters for real-time detection to work at all. Slight edge to B.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Swap theme dictionaries without destroying app styles
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct, avoid Clear(), and preserve template dictionaries. B directly matches the rubric's 'keep a reference' approach with a stored field, uses the typed dictionary constructors (avoiding path/Uri fragility), and adds a nice-to-have persistence via Preferences. A's string-matching approach works but is more brittle and doesn't hold a reference. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers with an exact, version-derived package list and a credible manifest/dependency-discovery path. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: B matches the essential diagnosis and remedy: the distribution vendor matters, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK should be installed and selected, and Temurin JAVA_HOME should not force the build to use it. A's core diagnosis and recommended configuration would preserve the actual incompatibility.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the requested safety posture and rubric: it avoids update/repair, uses an explicit matching workload version, and gives a clean diagnose-discover-reinstall-validate flow. A contains several valuable practical diagnostics, especially Android paths and cache handling, but its recommendation to run repair first and potentially update conflicts with the core requested approach.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: B is materially more actionable and version-specific, identifies the supported JDK distribution, uses maui-android appropriately for Linux, and grounds its dependency versions in official workload metadata. A has a broadly plausible outline but is less precise and weak on the supported-JDK and authoritative-version-discovery requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: B is somewhat more complete on dynamically determining Android and JDK requirements and explicitly covers Microsoft OpenJDK and required SDK packages. It is overly intricate and leaves some placeholder expansion/manual download work, but A has more consequential gaps and misleading implications that the MAUI workload itself provisions the Android SDK/emulator.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies nearly all requested setup-versioning safeguards: pinned workload installation, developer-download Xcode, supported Microsoft JDK, current official-source version discovery, and end-to-end checks. A is broadly useful but is materially weaker on version control and recommends workload updating.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and concisely satisfies every requested point. A is polished but materially misdirects the user by endorsing/configuring the Temurin path rather than recommending Microsoft OpenJDK and avoiding unnecessary JAVA_HOME overrides.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses give genuinely authoritative, non-guessing answers. A's GetAndroidDependencies MSBuild approach is elegant, simple, and robust for CI. B's WorkloadDependencies.json manifest approach is the deepest canonical source and best explains the SDK-version-to-manifest-to-Android-requirements relationship, which is central to the task, and directly produces the exact package list for sdkmanager. B's version-string manipulation is somewhat fragile, but its conceptual precision and explanation of the version chain give it a slight edge overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: The correct answer is that .NET MAUI on macOS expects the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and Temurin is the problem. Response B nails all four rubric criteria. Response A fundamentally misdiagnoses the issue as a version compatibility problem, incorrectly claims Temurin is supported, and tells the user to keep JAVA_HOME pointed at Temurin — failing every criterion. B is much better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns with best practice by explicitly discouraging workload update/repair and recommending versioned workload-set reinstalls, and it grounds versions in the authoritative workload manifest and live release metadata. A contradicts the key guidance by calling workload update 'generally safe' and recommending it, which is the exact concern the user raised. Both are well-structured, but B is materially more correct on the central point."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all four rubric criteria, correctly advising against both commands and recommending pinned reinstallation with a version-discovery method. A recommends the opposite approach (running repair first) and misses every criterion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, methodical plans that correctly restrict to Android on Linux and avoid iOS/Mac Catalyst. B is superior on the Microsoft OpenJDK requirement (A gets this wrong by recommending generic openjdk), explicitly warns against the maui meta-workload and workload update, and provides a rigorous dynamic version-discovery process. A's InstallAndroidDependencies approach is practical but less aligned with the rubric's JDK and dynamic-discovery emphasis. B edges out A across most criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are thorough, well-structured, dynamic-version-oriented plans. Neither uses the ideal 'dotnet workload search' CLI approach; both query the external releases-index.json. B distinguishes itself by discovering JDK and Android SDK requirements from the local WorkloadDependencies.json manifest — tying installed versions to what the actual MAUI workload demands, which is more correct than A's 'pick the newest available platform/build-tools' heuristic that could install mismatched versions. B also correctly emphasizes Microsoft OpenJDK. A has some advantages (cleaner emulator/AVD setup, developer mode, cleaner maui workload handling) and both are strong, so the gap is only slight.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are well-structured, thorough setup plans with official sources and verification steps. However, B aligns much more closely with the rubric's emphasis on dynamic version discovery, pinned reproducible workloads, avoiding hardcoded versions, warning about Xcode auto-update risks, and avoiding 'workload update/repair'. A is a solid, readable guide but relies on hardcoded versions (.NET 10, MAUI 10, JDK 17), unpinned workload installs, recommends the App Store for Xcode without the auto-update warning, and suggests 'dotnet workload update'. B wins on 5 of 6 criteria, several decisively.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly identifies that the Stack Overflow fix (setting JAVA_HOME to Temurin) is not the right approach, explains MAUI auto-detects supported JDKs, warns Temurin is not supported, and recommends Microsoft OpenJDK. A largely endorses the Stack Overflow approach, treating setting JAVA_HOME as correct and only cautioning the path may not exist—missing the key point that Temurin is the wrong distribution and JAVA_HOME isn't required. B satisfies 3 of 4 criteria strongly while A satisfies essentially only the OpenJDK recommendation.

The responses are close; B edges ahead on the central dynamic-versioning requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: A is modestly stronger because it points to the concrete authoritative manifest and provides a more informative extraction of required versus optional dependencies. Both answers give the correct observed core package list, but both generic automation snippets have correctness flaws that prevent a large advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the central vendor-specific fix. A is modestly less harmful because it does not incorrectly insist that JDK 17 is too new and acknowledges that the selected build JDK may differ from the shell runtime; B's asserted JDK-11 prescription is an unsupported and likely incorrect diagnosis for the stated setup.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: A is the more complete and actionable diagnostic/recovery plan, especially for Android and post-fix validation. Both miss the rubric's key request to avoid repair and reinstall workloads pinned to explicitly determined versions, so the advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the central required guidance and recommend the commands the rubric says to caution against. B is only marginally more useful because its update/restore/build flow and SDK inspection step provide a slightly better diagnostic follow-up.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more reliable for this Linux-only MAUI Android scenario: it avoids the unsupported MAUI meta-workload, mandates the correct Java distribution, and gives a specific official mechanism to discover exact versions. A has useful general setup steps but contains two consequential wrong recommendations.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more directly actionable for a Windows setup: it includes the required `sdkmanager.bat` form, explicitly searches workloads through the dotnet CLI, and consistently uses the umbrella MAUI workload. Both have notable version hardcoding and some questionable setup details, so the gap is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: A is somewhat more actionable and complete for the core setup: it gives the correct `maui` workload command, includes Xcode first-run/license steps, and uses version-agnostic sample build verification. Both miss key reproducibility/Java/Xcode-update guidance and both incorrectly present retired Visual Studio for Mac as an option; B also includes brittle net8 target examples and an overstated Apple-ID claim.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers miss the core MAUI-specific guidance: JAVA_HOME is generally unnecessary due to auto-detection, and explicitly pointing it at a non-Microsoft JDK may create failures; neither recommends Microsoft OpenJDK. A is modestly preferable because it cautions against blindly hardcoding the path, while B more affirmatively promotes the unsupported direction.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns closely with all requested diagnostic and remediation criteria, especially manifest-driven version discovery, pinned workload reinstall, and repeated validation. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration

A contains some useful cautions about hardcoded paths and GUI environment inheritance, but its recommendation to dynamically set JAVA_HOME undermines the central compatibility guidance.

activationScenarios.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
Guardrail against workload update and repair
Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: B supplies the intended vendor-specific diagnosis and actionable fix, whereas A declines to diagnose and incorrectly treats Temurin as acceptable while offering generic, mostly irrelevant troubleshooting.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the requested safe strategy of discovering compatible requirements and installing explicitly rather than blindly updating or repairing. However, it is incomplete and weakly actionable, makes questionable JDK claims, and is distracted by an unrelated Linux execution environment. A is more command-oriented but includes misleading/nonstandard diagnostics and unsafe or contrary workload guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the requested recovery strategy: it diagnoses the installed SDK/workload state and provides a pinned workload installation rather than suggesting update or repair. A gives the opposite recommendation and contains unsupported claims about SDK updates corrupting workloads.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: B better satisfies the key Linux MAUI requirements by explicitly selecting `maui-android`, excluding Apple targets, using Microsoft OpenJDK, and placing command-line tools in the standard `cmdline-tools/latest` layout. It still has important shortcomings—unjustified hardcoded versions, a likely missing Microsoft package-repository prerequisite, and incomplete authoritative version discovery. A has some useful project-version discovery advice but its non-Microsoft JDK recommendation and incorrect command-line-tools PATH/layout make the proposed setup less reliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: B better addresses the core request for dynamically determined, compatible SDK, workload, JDK, and Android dependency versions, while retaining the correct cross-platform MAUI workload. It still has practical gaps (notably bootstrap/order concerns and an incomplete scripted JDK installation), so the overall advantage is not overwhelming. A is more conventionally concrete in places, but its many stale hardcoded versions, broken command-line-tools move, Windows-incompatible `grep`, and incomplete Visual Studio workload command materially undermine a from-scratch plan.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: B supplies the essential `maui` workload installation and verification step that A entirely omits, making B materially more likely to yield a functioning clean-machine MAUI setup. Both have important shortcomings around supported Java distribution, reproducible pinning, and Xcode update control, but A's missing workload is a fundamental gap.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B addresses all of the requested technical points and reaches the intended recommendation. Its assertion that the user is on Linux and its apt commands conflict with the stated macOS scenario, but those are ancillary errors; A's central guidance is incompatible with the rubric throughout.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid legacy Xamarin.Forms lifecycle methods
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the correct Window-based MAUI lifecycle approach, accurate central mappings, and practical implementation examples. A’s central Application-event recommendation undermines its otherwise simple mapping.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Platform-specific lifecycle mapping
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the requested .NET MAUI mechanism with usable platform-specific callbacks and a correct cross-platform Window alternative. A contains a major misleading/nonexistent App.Stopping recommendation and its native snippets are less integrated and incomplete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Save and restore state on background
judgeRationales.rationale: B uses the appropriate Window lifecycle events, covers the Android destruction edge case, and provides a coherent integration example. A's central claim that page appearing/disappearing reliably represent app foreground/background is incorrect and its final answer merely references files rather than showing a robust app-lifecycle solution.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Window lifecycle event subscription
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the correct, practical per-window subscription pattern and the correct six event names. Although it omits the initial-launch Resumed caveat, it is substantially more accurate and useful than A, whose central event names and subscription timing are flawed.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid ListView and ViewCell mistakes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are correct, concise, and provide an effective before/after migration example. B is marginally stronger for its unambiguous statement that ViewCell is unsupported, explicit replacement options, and useful compiled-binding suggestion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Basic CollectionView with data binding and DataTemplate
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the more usable compiled-binding example because its XAML namespaces and root x:DataType are complete, whereas A's undefined local prefix is a build-breaking omission. B does have a minor erroneous duplicate Name binding in a label labeled Price, preventing a larger advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Grid layout with CollectionView
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies the requested three-column grid using the correct Span property and supplies a coherent MAUI page example. A's use of Columns instead of Span is a central functional XAML error, despite otherwise covering spacing and the item template.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: ItemSizingStrategy placement for uniform items
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the .NET MAUI CollectionView question with correct XAML and accurate limitations. A substitutes unrelated framework-specific virtualization settings and therefore misses the central requested API.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Selection and pull-to-refresh with CollectionView
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies the request with usable XAML, ViewModel code, and binding explanations. A's final answer omits the promised code entirely and points to local files the user cannot access. B has a minor practical DI issue—its XAML directly constructs a ViewModel with constructor dependencies—but it remains vastly more complete and actionable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create and use an IValueConverter
judgeRationales.rationale: A and B deliver the core converter equally well, but A provides a more complete, valid XAML setup. B's omitted x and vm namespace declarations make its otherwise sound sample fail as presented.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose missing BindingContext and non-compiled bindings
judgeRationales.rationale: Both find the core issue, but B supplies a valid XAML setup, includes the requested compiled-binding guidance, and avoids A's invalid XAML instantiation suggestion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement MVVM ViewModel with ObservableObject
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers with usable ViewModel, command, package requirement, and binding examples. Although its XAML refers to an undefined inverted-boolean converter and uses @ in prose for C# attributes, its central implementation is sound. A's final response is only a status summary of inaccessible claimed files, so it fails to show the requested implementation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up compiled bindings with x:DataType on a page

B does contain an overstatement that a nonexistent-property binding yields XC0022, and it omits NativeAOT/trimming discussion, but is still substantially stronger. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid AddScoped pitfall in MAUI
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly satisfies all requested lifetime points, particularly the explicit singleton-like behavior and intended sharing alternative. A is mostly correct and offers a solid scoped-operation wrapper, but its recommendation to EnsureDeleted/EnsureCreated to clear navigation state is unsafe and conceptually wrong for preserving application data.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose a page whose injected dependencies are missing
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the correct distinction between ContentTemplate activation and registered-route navigation and offers the requested viable remedies. It unnecessarily says registering the page itself is required, but that minor imprecision does not outweigh A's wholesale reversal of both mechanisms and incorrect fix.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Platform-specific service registration with fallback
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers with correct, usable MauiProgram registration code, includes Mac Catalyst, and supplies a no-op fallback. A is mostly a high-level description, refers to inaccessible generated files, and its partial-class approach omits Mac Catalyst and fallback coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Register services with correct lifetimes in MauiProgram.cs
judgeRationales.rationale: Both convey the recommended lifetime pattern correctly, but B actually supplies the central registration code the user asked to see. Its extra Shell discussion is not essential, while A's missing code is a meaningful omission.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Shell navigation auto-resolves DI-registered pages
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all requested wiring steps, particularly transient registrations and explicit Routing.RegisterRoute, and gives a clear end-to-end resolution chain. A has the required page constructor but uses incorrect lifetimes for the rubric and substitutes a ShellContent DataTemplate pattern for explicit route registration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid deprecated UseSafeArea in new .NET 10 project
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately answers both migration questions using the .NET 10 SafeAreaEdges API and examples. A gets only the UseSafeArea deprecation directionally right, but materially misleads by endorsing obsolete IgnoreSafeArea and omitting SafeAreaEdges.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Edge-to-edge layout with SafeAreaEdges
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately explains and demonstrates the .NET 10 solution. A misdiagnoses the padding, omits the essential child-layout setting, and adds a legacy UseSafeArea recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Handle notch and status bar safe areas on iOS
judgeRationales.rationale: B precisely answers the migration question: SafeAreaEdges="Container" is shown as the direct replacement, along with the legacy/obsolete and cross-platform context. A supplies a usable but overly broad All setting and misleadingly frames the legacy API mainly as backward-compatible.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keyboard avoidance with safe area for chat UI
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the .NET 10 problem with the correct SafeAreaEdges and SoftInput pattern and usable XAML. A lacks that API entirely and includes unsupported or misleading alternatives, so it would not reliably solve the stated issue.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +80.0% (4W/1T/0L over 5 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.063), mean preference +56.0% across 5 paired run(s) — not credible — 1 of 5 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s) tied, leaving only 4 discordant preference vote(s). The sign test conditions on non-tie stimulus votes and cannot reach 0.05 below 5, so no record could have passed here — this is not a measured null. Either the skill is inert on these scenarios (make them discriminate) or the eval needs more distinct stimuli to clear the ties

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose common Shell navigation mistakes
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly addresses the two key Shell-routing concepts targeted by the prompt—RegisterRoute for a standalone relative route and full visual-hierarchy matching for an absolute route—while also giving the correct lazy ContentTemplate startup guidance. A gets the startup advice right but substantially misfocuses the first two diagnoses.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Handle back navigation and unsaved changes guard
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly provides the core Shell implementation, including cancellation, async deferral, Pop filtering, and custom back-button text. Its explicit BackCommand can cause a second confirmation when it subsequently calls GoToAsync because the Shell guard still sees unsaved changes, so it should centralize/bypass the second guard; nevertheless it is far more complete and technically aligned than A's code-free, incomplete outline.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Navigate with parameters using GoToAsync
judgeRationales.rationale: B best satisfies the explicit full-object requirement by using ShellNavigationQueryParameters and otherwise provides the requested VM-based reception. Its CollectionView SelectionChanged command-parameter binding is questionable for a method expecting Product, whereas A's direct tapped-product handler is clearer, so the overall advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Shell navigation with tabs and flyout
judgeRationales.rationale: B substantially better satisfies the requested Shell design and correctly performs detail-route registration. Both final answers are seriously deficient because they merely summarize files rather than showing the requested AppShell.xaml, but A additionally lacks the required constructor registration and appears to use an unsuitable TabBar-based hierarchy. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stable routes for deep linking into tabs
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

activationScenarios.scenarioName: Add light/dark mode support using AppThemeBinding
Avoid common theming mistakes
Create custom themes with ResourceDictionary switching
Detect and respond to system theme changes
Swap theme dictionaries without destroying app styles

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add light/dark mode support using AppThemeBinding
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the request with usable XAML, explains automatic system-theme response, and gives the requested C# extension-method alternative. A's final output is only an unsupported summary of files allegedly created, leaving the user without the actual code or explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid common theming mistakes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solve the DynamicResource issue, but B also correctly solves the Android restart with the required UiMode activity configuration and gives directly usable code. A's Android guidance misses the actual cause and proposes dubious lifecycle configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create custom themes with ResourceDictionary switching
judgeRationales.rationale: B presents the correct central mechanism for immediate multi-theme updates: DynamicResource consumers plus replacement of only the active theme dictionary. It has a minor omission—the Picker event is not wired in its XAML—but A's StaticResource advice and clearing all merged dictionaries are fundamental defects for this task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect and respond to system theme changes
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately uses RequestedTheme for current system-theme detection and clearly applies UserAppTheme only as the override. A's central service has a substantive semantic bug in system-default mode, returning and logging Unspecified or an old override instead of the actual requested system theme.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Swap theme dictionaries without destroying app styles
judgeRationales.rationale: B most directly meets the central requirement of tracking and swapping only the active theme dictionary, while preserving Colors.xaml and Styles.xaml. A is a viable Source-based alternative, but it does not satisfy the requested reference-tracking pattern and is less exact.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create custom themes with ResourceDictionary switching
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses provide fundamentally sound solutions for theme switching in .NET MAUI. Response A uses a clean dependency-injection pattern with a service interface, while Response B uses a static helper class. Both approach is valid. However, Response B excels in clarity and completeness: (1) it explicitly shows the x:Class and code-behind structure for ResourceDictionaries, answering a critical implementation question that Response A only implies, (2) it uses a more sophisticated dictionary swapping strategy (Remove then Add vs Clear), (3) it includes bonus features like system theme detection and Android platform-specific configuration, and (4) it provides more detailed example color definitions. Response A's main strength is its explicit MVVM/DI pattern, which some developers prefer, but this doesn't outweigh Response B's superior coverage of the loading mechanism and additional best practices."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect and respond to system theme changes
judgeRationales.rationale: While both responses cover all four rubric criteria equally, Response B provides a significantly more production-ready and complete solution. Response B includes: (1) Preference persistence using Preferences.Get/Set, which is essential for user theme overrides to actually persist across app launches; (2) Better code organization via a ThemeService static class; (3) Critical Android-specific configuration (ConfigChanges.UiMode) for proper theme change handling; (4) Complete initialization logic that restores saved preferences on startup. Response A correctly covers the basic APIs but is more minimal and omits these practical considerations necessary for a real-world implementation. For a developer implementing this, Response B provides a ready-to-use pattern that would work correctly across platforms and app sessions."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Swap theme dictionaries without destroying app styles
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly better because it directly addresses the core rubric requirement of keeping a reference to the current theme (Criterion 3), which Response A fails to do. Response A's filename-matching approach is a workaround that introduces unnecessary fragility by depending on the Source property being set predictably on dynamic ResourceDictionary instances. Response B's approach is the idiomatic, robust pattern for runtime resource management. Additionally, Response B includes theme persistence and better error handling as bonuses. Both responses avoid the critical mistake of calling Clear(), but Response B is the correct, production-ready solution." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the correct manifest-derived package list, but A provides a substantially more usable, working CI-oriented extraction method. B's explicit MAUI relationship is a small clarity advantage, but its broken path construction materially undermines the requested programmatic solution.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the essential Microsoft-JDK vendor diagnosis and provide an incorrect Temurin-based remedy. B is marginally better because it includes valid checks for JAVA_HOME/JDK completeness and frames its version claim less categorically, but it still would not reliably fix the stated issue.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B much more closely matches the requested/rubric safe remediation approach: it avoids broad update/repair initially, uses version-specific workload installation, and gives a structured validation path across SDK, JDK, Android packages, and build results. A contains several useful checks but its central recommendation to run repair then update conflicts with the intended approach.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: B better fulfills the central request to determine correct versions dynamically and adheres to the Linux MAUI support requirement for Microsoft OpenJDK. A is more directly copy-pastable in places, but its unsupported Java recommendation and arbitrary hardcoded Android/NDK versions are material setup risks.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more complete operationally: it includes concrete MAUI install/restore commands, target build commands, Android configuration checks, and more detailed device/signing guidance. Both have a serious currentness problem in recommending Visual Studio 2022 for Mac despite its retirement, and both miss workload pinning and the required strict Microsoft-OpenJDK guidance. B is somewhat better on naming Microsoft OpenJDK, but not enough to outweigh A's more actionable verification plan.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose a page whose injected dependencies are missing
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately distinguishes XAML ContentTemplate activation from DI-aware Shell route activation and gives the appropriate registration/navigation fix. A gets the ContentTemplate behavior right but makes a central factual error about GoToAsync route construction, so it fails the key contrast in the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Platform-specific service registration with fallback
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are technically sound and safely use compile-time platform registration with a fallback. B is more complete for MAUI targets by explicitly handling Mac Catalyst and more clearly states why the fallback matters.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Register services with correct lifetimes in MauiProgram.cs
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers substantially satisfy the task with the same core lifetime choices. A is slightly more internally consistent because its concrete HTTP and data-service registrations actually preserve the advertised singleton service lifetime, whereas B's AddHttpClient typed-client suggestion can contradict it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Shell navigation auto-resolves DI-registered pages
judgeRationales.rationale: Both meet every core requirement. A is slightly more complete and focused as an end-to-end wiring chain because it also shows registering and injecting AppShell into App before navigation. B's optional IDataService/query example introduces an unregistered dependency and extra detail that is not needed for the requested wiring.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Edge-to-edge layout with SafeAreaEdges

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Determine required Android SDK packages for specific .NET version
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the exact current package IDs from the installed workload's authoritative dependency metadata and a practical way to regenerate them in CI. A is directionally aware of manifests and targets but fails to give a dependable extraction path and includes likely inaccurate auto-provisioning guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the requested root cause and a directly actionable, vendor-specific remediation. A offers plausible generic Java troubleshooting but fundamentally misses and contradicts the required Microsoft-JDK vendor constraint.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fix stale MAUI workloads after SDK update
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially better aligned with all requested remediation criteria: it avoids indiscriminate update/repair, identifies a matching pinned workload set, derives Android requirements from workload metadata, and validates the repaired environment. A offers generally plausible diagnostics but recommends the approaches the rubric specifically discourages and lacks a reliable version-pinning method.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all specified criteria: it warns against the two commands, recommends a concrete version-pinned reinstall, explains its consistency rationale, and derives the pin from the current SDK. A takes the opposite approach and omits version pinning.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan Linux MAUI environment for Android
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives a substantially more authoritative and actionable headless-Linux setup plan, including live workload-manifest version discovery and the required Microsoft OpenJDK constraint. A has the right workload and general SDK setup direction, but its Temurin recommendation is a material compatibility error and its version-selection method is less reliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan complete MAUI setup on Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan macOS MAUI setup with Xcode
judgeRationales.rationale: B delivers a materially more reliable and reproducible setup: it uses official version discovery, pins the workload set, correctly mandates Microsoft OpenJDK, and protects against Xcode auto-update incompatibilities. A has useful basics, but its App Store Xcode advice, missing JDK requirement, unpinned workload, and questionable .NET 9 guidance make it substantially less suitable for a clean-machine setup.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent incorrect JAVA_HOME configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly follows all requested guidance: reject the Temurin JAVA_HOME workaround, rely on MAUI detection, identify the non-Microsoft-JDK failure risk, and recommend Microsoft OpenJDK. A is more expansive but its central recommendation conflicts with those requirements and includes questionable, distracting JDK-location guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose non-Microsoft JDK causing build failure
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides a fundamentally correct diagnosis that aligns with all four rubric criteria: it correctly identifies JDK vendor as the root cause, recommends the Microsoft-supported OpenJDK, advises removing the Temurin configuration entirely, and makes clear that Adoptium is not acceptable for .NET MAUI. Response A misdiagnoses the problem as an environment/IDE detection issue and incorrectly suggests that Temurin JDK 17.0.12 is valid for .NET MAUI, which contradicts all four rubric criteria. This is not a marginal difference—the two responses give opposite guidance on the fundamental issue."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response B delivers a significantly more rigorous and authoritative diagnostic and remediation plan. It directly addresses the user's safety concern by strongly discouraging update/repair commands, provides concrete mechanisms to discover correct versions from authoritative sources (APIs and manifests), specifies exact Android SDK packages with verification procedures, includes Java/JDK alignment, and structures revalidation as an explicit phase. Response A provides a reasonable baseline but is permissive about unsafe commands, lacks version discovery mechanisms, omits Java considerations, and provides only generic Android guidance. For a technical problem requiring precision and safety, Response B's comprehensiveness and specificity represent a substantial quality advantage."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Guardrail against workload update and repair
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly better. It correctly identifies that the user's .NET SDK was updated but workloads were not installed (or removed), making neither `update` nor `repair` the appropriate solution. Response B explicitly warns against the approaches the user was considering and provides the correct recovery path: explicit workload installation with version pinning. Response A recommends the wrong first step (`dotnet workload update`) and fails to warn against it, missing the fundamental issue. Response B's investigation-based approach also discovered concrete facts about the environment (SDK 10.0.401, no installed workloads), whereas Response A provided generic advice without environment verification."

judgeRationales.rationale: A is materially closer because it uses the correct BackButtonBehavior label property and includes an _isLeaving guard to prevent its confirmation-triggered GoToAsync from being intercepted again. Both omit the proper deferral pattern, and both have a command-binding inconsistency: their primary XAML bindings target a view model while the substantive cancel command is shown on the page.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Navigate with parameters using GoToAsync
judgeRationales.rationale: A correctly demonstrates receiving both parameter forms in a view-model IQueryAttributable implementation and supplies a practical CollectionView handler. It misses the explicit ShellNavigationQueryParameters type, but B has the more serious architectural and interface-signature errors and does not use the requested full-object payload approach.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Shell navigation with tabs and flyout
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers satisfy all explicit requirements. A is slightly cleaner and more internally consistent: its XAML page namespace matches its code-behind import and it uses a clearly named ActiveProductsPage. B's direct Settings ShellContent is valid, but its XAML references pages in MyMauiApp while the code-behind imports MyMauiApp.Views, creating an avoidable namespace ambiguity.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stable routes for deep linking into tabs
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly answers the stated FlyoutItem/Tab/ShellContent scenario, provides the complete explicit hierarchy and corresponding absolute URI, and gives the clearer explanation of why implicit routes are brittle. Both miss the requested D_FAULT_ naming detail, so the advantage is limited.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +40.0% (3W/1T/1L over 5 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.312), mean preference +16.0% across 5 paired run(s) — not credible — 1 of 5 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s) tied, leaving only 4 discordant preference vote(s). The sign test conditions on non-tie stimulus votes and cannot reach 0.05 below 5, so no record could have passed here — this is not a measured null. Either the skill is inert on these scenarios (make them discriminate) or the eval needs more distinct stimuli to clear the ties

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add light/dark mode support using AppThemeBinding
judgeRationales.rationale: A directly fulfills both requested approaches and correctly uses AppTheme.Unspecified to follow the OS. B's XAML is good, but its C# alternative misses the requested MAUI theme extension and AppTheme.FollowSystem is not a valid AppTheme value in standard .NET MAUI.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Avoid common theming mistakes
judgeRationales.rationale: B better addresses runtime resource switching via DynamicResource and more nearly explains the configuration-change issue. Both omit the crucial concrete ConfigChanges.UiMode Activity attribute, and B includes some unnecessary Android/AppCompat guidance, so the advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create custom themes with ResourceDictionary switching
judgeRationales.rationale: Both convey the core DynamicResource and persistence pattern, but B is a coherent, safer implementable solution. A has a material runtime/compilation inconsistency around dictionary construction and destructively clears all merged dictionaries.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect and respond to system theme changes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are accurate, complete answers to the requested APIs and include real-time handling, logging, override, and reset examples. A has more production-appropriate ILogger usage, while B has more concrete theme-aware UI binding examples; neither has a meaningful overall quality advantage. Both also omit platform-specific caveats such as Android configuration handling, so neither gains an edge there.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Swap theme dictionaries without destroying app styles
judgeRationales.rationale: Both use the right general selective-merge approach and preserve template styles, but B's added dictionary carries the Source used by its removal logic. Neither implements the requested explicit current-theme reference, and B assumes a folder path not supplied, so the advantage is modest.
